title: Generic Powered Parachute — Normal Operating Procedures (FAA Powered Parachute Flying Handbook)
description: A type-generic normal-operations checklist for certificated powered parachutes (PPC), assembled from the FAA Powered Parachute Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-12A), a US Government work in the public domain. Covers preflight documentation check, walk-around, engine start, warm-up, wing layout, before-takeoff, takeoff, cruise, approach, and shutdown. Not a substitute for the specific POH/AFM of any individual aircraft: the Handbook itself directs the pilot to the aircraft's own checklist. Items follow the sequence and wording of Chapters 5, 7, and adjacent sections of the source document.

source.title: Powered Parachute Flying Handbook
source.publisher: U.S. Department of Transportation, Federal Aviation Administration, Flight Standards Service
source.notes: The Handbook presents procedures as prose text rather than a formal challenge/response checklist. Converting prose to challenge/response pairs is an editorial act by the transcriber; item text follows the Handbook's wording as closely as practical. The PAVE and LOC acronyms and the five-task walk-around structure (cart, powerplant, equipment, engine warm-up, wing) are taken directly from the source. All values in this file are generic; the pilot must consult the POH for the specific PPC being flown for numeric limits.

known_issues.description: Type-generic by construction. Every aircraft-specific limit (RPM, CHT, EGT, fuel type, oil ratio, fuel quantity) is absent; consult the POH for the PPC being flown.
The Handbook covers single-engine PPCs. Twin-engine PPCs (such as the PM-2) have additional considerations for engine synchronisation and single-engine handling not covered here.
The Handbook's prose procedures have been converted to challenge/response format by the transcriber. Wording may not match the pilot's POH.

items.text: Before going to the field, evaluate the PAVE factors: Pilot, Aircraft, enVironment, External pressures. Establish personal minimums for each factor before proceeding.
Pilot (experience, currency, rest, illness, medication, stress)
Aircraft (fuel, weight within limits, density altitude, required equipment)
enVironment (weather at departure, route, destination; NOTAMs; TFRs)
External pressures (schedules, purpose of flight, perceived expectations)
Weather: wind speed and direction, gusts, thermals, convective activity
Density altitude
The following certificates and documents must be on board when the aircraft is operated. The mnemonic AROW: Airworthiness certificate, Registration, Operating limitations, Weight and balance.
Airworthiness certificate
Registration certificate
Operating limitations (AFM/POH, placards, or instrument markings)
Weight and balance data
Pilot certificate and photo ID (or valid driver's licence for Sport Pilots)
Aircraft logbooks (not required on board, but review for required inspections)

The PPC walk-around covers five tasks: (1) cart inspection, (2) powerplant inspection, (3) equipment check, (4) engine warm-up and check, (5) wing and suspension line inspection. Perform in a consistent, systematic sequence every flight.
Cart
Nosewheel: play, tire inflation, axle bolt
Ground steering bar connections and range of motion
Front fork to nosewheel and gooseneck connections
Brakes (if installed): cable or hydraulic, pads, alignment, no leaks
Pilot seat, rails, seat belt attachment points
items.response: SECURE, NO CRACKS, SEAT PIN LOCKED

items.text: Ignition and battery switches
Primer or primer bulb (if equipped)
Throttle control: full range of motion, no binding
Altimeter: set to field elevation or barometric pressure (if equipped)
Engine instrument master ON: note fuel quantity indication
Airframe: distortion, wear points, loose bolts, cable kinks or frays
Rear wheels, axle, tires: inflation, cuts, wear, wheel rotation
Fuel and oil
Fuel: type, grade, and quantity — visually confirm tank level matches gauge
items.detail: Check engine manufacturer's recommendation for fuel type and, on two-stroke engines, oil-to-fuel premix ratio. Incorrect ratio causes seizure.

items.text: Fuel sample: color, clarity, no water
Oil level and type (four-stroke, or two-stroke oil injection reservoir)
Powerplant
Treat the propeller as live at all times. Keep the propeller arc clear during all ground operations.
Propeller blades: cracks, chips, nicks; blade bolts secure
Engine area: clear of loose items that could enter propeller arc
Carburetor(s): secure; air filter condition and fit
Rubber manifolds: no cracks
Spark plug caps: secure on all cylinders
Gear reduction box: no leaking seals, no play in gears
Fuel lines: no fuel dye staining (indicates leakage), no deterioration
Oil lines and drain plug: no leaks, cap secure
Exhaust system: no white staining (exhaust leaks), springs secure, no cracks
Cooling system (liquid-cooled engines): coolant level, overflow reservoir
All visible wires and lines: security and condition
Perform wing inspection before every flight. The wing is as critical to airworthiness as the engine. Inspect methodically in the same order each time.
Wind direction
Wing removed from bag: not twisted, rotated, or turned
Wing fabric: tears, burns, abrasions, UV deterioration, cell debris
Wing laid out centered behind cart — "X" in suspension lines directly behind prop centerline
Riser cables at cart attachment: not twisted around airframe, secure links finger-tight plus quarter-turn
A-lines separated from B-lines at riser connection; A/C lines on top of B/D lines
Suspension lines: no tangles, knots, pressure knots, or broken strands; lines not wrapped over top of wing
items.detail: A line-over is a line that goes over the top of the wing rather than straight to the riser. It will prevent proper inflation and is a no-go item. Inspect the leading edge and top surface carefully.

items.text: A line-over causes catastrophic wing deformation on inflation. Do not launch with any line-over present.
Steering lines: clear of suspension lines, anchor knots secure, lines flow freely through guides and pulleys
Line-over check: no line over top surface of wing
Debris around wing and lines: ground clear of twigs, sticks, and objects that could cause pressure knots
Front wheels
Area behind cart and in propeller arc
Wing lines
Anti-collision strobe (if independent switch)
Fuel system: prime as equipped
Throttle
Call "CLEAR PROP" — wait for clear response from bystanders before starting
Magneto switches
Engine gauge master switch
Start engine — keep one hand on throttle
Oil pressure (if applicable)
items.detail: If oil pressure does not rise to manufacturer's specified value within a few seconds, shut down immediately to prevent engine damage.

items.text: Starter engaged warning light (if equipped)
Never skip the engine warm-up. Running a cold engine at high power is a leading cause of engine damage on two-stroke and four-stroke engines alike.
Idle warm-up: allow engine to reach minimum operating temperature
items.detail: Minimum warm-up time is per the engine manufacturer's POH. In temperatures below 50°F, extend warm-up time. Monitor CHT.

items.text: Engine gauges
items.response: TEMPERATURES AND PRESSURES IN NORMAL RANGE

items.text: Area behind cart still clear
Advance throttle to approximately 75% — hold 10 seconds
Ignition system check (dual ignition): switch one off, check RPM, restore; then alternate
items.response: BOTH CIRCUITS OPERATIONAL, RPM DROP WITHIN LIMITS

items.text: RPM at run-up power
Engine temperatures (CHT, EGT) at run-up
items.response: WITHIN LIMITS — DO NOT FLY IF ABNORMAL

items.text: Throttle to idle — engine settles smoothly
The before-takeoff check is the final systematic check of engine, controls, systems, and avionics before flight. It is also a go/no-go decision point.
Engine temperatures: confirm still within minimums since warm-up
Wind direction
items.response: RECHECKED — TAKEOFF POSITION CONFIRMED INTO WIND

items.text: Steering and suspension lines: not in path of tires, not tangled in riser cables
Seat belt and shoulder harness
Seat position (if adjustable)
Loose items: nothing able to enter propeller arc
Wire routing (GPS, intercom, headsets): does not interfere with controls
Strobe lights
Electric fuel pump (if applicable)
Fuel quantity
Ignition system check (final)
Traffic pattern and intended takeoff runway/area
Radio call or traffic scan (as applicable)
Passenger briefing (if passenger aboard)
items.response: COMPLETE — SEATBELTS, EMERGENCY PROCEDURES, HANDS AND FEET INSIDE

sections.title: Takeoff Roll — Wing Inflation and LOC Check

items.text: LOC: L — Lines Free; O — Cells Open; C — Wing Centered. Do not advance to takeoff thrust until the wing passes the LOC check.
Throttle: advance smoothly to one-half to two-thirds takeoff power
items.detail: Too abrupt an application yanks the wing forward and can damage the riser system.

items.text: Feet on steering bars throughout takeoff roll
Wing inflating and rising: correct for any side that rises faster
If a line-over is visible (wing pinched and deformed), shut down immediately and re-lay the wing. Do not continue the takeoff roll.
LOC check: Lines free
LOC check: all Cells open including end cells
LOC check: Wing Centered overhead, forward to riser attachment points
Advance throttle to takeoff thrust
Directional control during ground roll
After liftoff: maintain full power and climb away from ground
Initial climb path: aligned with takeoff direction — clear of obstacles
Engine temperatures during climb
items.detail: On a hot day or at density altitude, allow CHT to stabilize before sustained climbs. Reduce power if approaching limits.

items.text: Reduce to cruise power at safe maneuvering altitude
RPM
Engine temperatures: CHT and EGT
Avoid prolonged idle on two-stroke engines during descent. Make brief power additions every 30–60 seconds to prevent plug fouling and prevent CHT from dropping too rapidly.
Fuel endurance: note time and fuel remaining
items.detail: Consult POH for fuel burn and minimum reserve. Manage the flight so that you land with the required fuel reserve remaining — do not plan to land on fumes.

items.text: Approach: plan into wind where possible
Landing area: clear of obstacles, suitable surface
Airspeed: maintain above stall during entire approach
Avoid rapid throttle changes on approach. Rapid throttle movements cause pitch oscillations (porpoising). Use slow, smooth throttle inputs.
Throttle to idle on short final
Flare: begin approximately 1 second above the ground — push both foot steering bars smoothly forward
items.detail: Hold flare as rear wheels touch. Do not release flare when close to the ground without power — the canopy will surge forward and produce a dive.

items.text: After touchdown: release flare smoothly — collapse canopy immediately
Idle: allow engine to cool for at least 1 minute
Magneto switches
Propeller stopped: confirm before approaching
All electronics and instruments
Fuel valve (if applicable)
Canopy: fold, pack into wing bag, and secure
items.detail: Pack the canopy immediately after landing to protect from UV exposure and unexpected wind gusts. A free wing can be picked up by wind and drag the cart.

items.text: Fuel cap
Tie-down or hangar as required
